[Discussion] Do you think Tetris trademark should be genericized?
Hmmm. No? Maybe. I dunno. Would that mean King starts cranking out PTW versions of it? If yes then no. If no then yes. I still prefer the original NES version that had the Russian theme.

No, but I don't think any trademark should be made generic. Just because it's become popular enough to use in common language to cover a range of products shouldn't mean you lose legal protection over its use. It forces companies to zealously enforce their trademark so it doesn't become generic and hurts the rest of us.

With that logic, could Sims trademark the 'Sim' thing? I get that was kind of around before them, but when we think of playing the Sims- we think of just that. No one wld say 'lets play that realistic role playing game that's based on real life.'

There's sort of this unfortunate attitude within part of the gaming community that could be summarized as, "We don't like what you did with this so you should lose your rights to it so someone else can do better." Don't like the fact that one of your favorite games hasn't seen an update in 5 years? "At least make it open source." Don't like the latest Tetris offering? Take away the trademark.

That's not how things work. Nobody gets to come into your house and take away your TV because you haven't watched it in a week. They don't get to raid your cupboards because you've had the same can of tomato paste sitting there for over a year. They can't claim the title to your car because you haven't had it serviced...ever.

We have laws to protect ownership rights specifically in order to prevent people from behaving badly because they've decided that their arbitrary reason to ignore your rights is enough to have their way with your stuff. Entitled gamers don't get to ignore those laws because they don't understand or like IP rights. Leave registered trademarks alone.

Actually, trademarks are meant to protect the consumers. Since there are now easily-available reviews and let's plays out there, it seems that trademarks named after companies and their subsidiaries are useful. What good does a trademark of Tetris do to a consumer if the quality of official Tetris games is not consistent?

Trademarks are owned and protected by companies, not consumers. If the Tetris trademark has come to represent inconsistency, then it represents inconsistency. No trademark exists to assure quality, it exists to represent a brand. If the quality of the brand diminishes then so does the trademark. One way or another, it remains the property of the registered owner and the consumer has no rights to it. At all.
They're owned by companies but they're meant to protect consumers.

They're owned by companies. And you can't decide that you want to simply appropriate them because you don't like what the company has done. It's against the law.

That's the alpha and the omega of the entire discussion.

Period.
They're owned as long as it's not generic. However, people have used the term Tetris for Tetris clones long enough now for trademark to become meaningless.

People chatting in day to day discourse using the term "Tetris" doesn't diminish the trademark. Game developers coming out in droves calling their falling block puzzle game Tetris without an appropriate legal challenge from the owner would.

You'd benefit from ceasing to think that a disappointing game is justification for a crusade. Move on with your life. This is just stupid.
The concept is already not copyrighted. There's nothing stopping anyone from making a game with the same mechanics. Tetris clones are a popular project for beginner game design.

NO.

On one end, it would get the Tetris Company to stop enforcing that STUPID Tetris guideline and we'd finally be able to get a true Tetris: The Grand Master on consoles.

On the other, it would make other companies send more C&Ds to fan projects to protect their IPs. I think that they should END trademark genericization laws, because they hurt everyone.
Trademarks are not valuable to consumers when it comes to games and game series. Creator names are much better trademarks.
Yes, but if there were no trademark genericization laws, companies wouldn't be able to justify sending C&Ds to fan projects (see: Project M,) it would be a waste of their time and resources.

But the question is: are those trademarks worth keeping in the first place?

The law should be changed so that fans would decide if the fan project is not cancelled or not.
Why not just remove most trademark laws?
Because I still believe that companies should be able to own IP. I just think that we should remove laws that make non-profit fan projects a liability.
